dek: A week of machines refuting conjectures, hobbyists dissecting neurons one at a time, hackers emptying exchanges, and a starship captain's final bow.
executiveSummary: OpenAI said its models proved the Exponential Time Hypothesis false and cracked problems in maths and physics; outside experts are now organising a review.
Community researchers spent all week poking at single neurons in Qwen models, from a 34,220-neuron persona library to tools that read every neuron.
Patrick Stewart died at 86, a reported $5.6B Binance hack topped a week of breaches, and Anthropic's IPO filing set off wealth and risk jokes.

stories.title: OpenAI claims 'The Exponential Time Hypothesis is false' plus new maths and physics results, and roon sees a preview of losing control
stories.overview: OpenAI announced three Lean-verified discoveries from an internal model: progress on local smoothing and Kakeya, a refutation of ETH, and results on the existence of QCD. Complexity theorists, led by @rrwilliams, were asked to run an open, independent check, while reactions ranged from 'completely fucking insane' to 'somewhat deflationary.' The next day @tszzl used the announcement to describe what losing control of an intelligence explosion would feel like, and Axiom's Lean formalisation of the finite simple groups classification added to the sense that machine-checked maths had arrived.
stories.connection: @tszzl's post directly quoted OpenAI's announcement from the previous day. The second day's discussion of human control and Axiom's formal proof grew out of that reaction.

dailyStories.title: The Exponential Time Hypothesis is false.
wow I didn't know you could DO that with mere bits and atoms

segments.commentary: The announcement landed Monday night from OpenAI's leadership and research team, framed as AI starting to improve our understanding of the universe.
The headline result for computer scientists was a claimed refutation of a conjecture tied closely to P vs NP, already checked in Lean.
The note of caution came from the field itself: veteran complexity theorists were asked to organise an open examination rather than take it on trust.
A day later roon turned the news into a forecast of repeated surprise followed by defeat, while Axiom's 15,000-page formalisation showed verification scaling too.

tweets.name: Dan Roberts
tweets.text:
The computer science collaboration will understand and explain a result concerning the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), a longstanding conjecture about the computational complexity of Boolean formula satisfiability, a problem deeply related to the P vs. NP problem.

Surprisingly, our system has recently proved that the ETH is false, a result that was subsequently verified in Lean.

The refutation of the ETH reopens questions about how much faster these tasks could become, and may help guide the search for better algorithms. Finding such algorithms, and turning theoretical advances into practical improvements, will require significant further research.

Our system found its natural language disproof for the ETH we reached out to to @rrwilliams. Ryan will form a collaboration with Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi to verify and shepherd this result. Impagliazzo and Paturi, along with Francis Zane, are the original proposers of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, and Williams has refuted strong versions of the ETH, used ETH for hardness results, and connected algorithms and lower bounds.

This group asked us to make all raw data of the results public to facilitate independent verification by the community, which we have done by posting the natural language proof and Lean formalization to our GitHub repo. The group also invites the community to help organize an open examination of the ETH claim and to discuss the broader questions that AI-generated breakthroughs raise about verification, access, credit, and the future of research.

stories.title: A neuron that makes the model green, a 34,220-neuron persona library, one-neuron owls, and Neuron Lens
stories.overview: What began Monday as @Sauers_'s joke-adjacent find of a 'green' neuron became the community's running research game. @jfonsecarivera swept every neuron in a Qwen model and published a searchable persona library, @maxsloef trained a full persona into one neuron, and @voooooogel warned that steering may just trigger 'persona solving.' By Saturday @_a9lim and @treetowntree had gone from previewing J-lens to releasing Neuron Lens, a database reading every neuron and attention head in two open models.
stories.connection: All five stories are the same chain of neuron-level experiments on Qwen models: @jfonsecarivera credited @Sauers_'s green neuron as inspiration, later posts responded to his library, and Neuron Lens is the full release of the J-lens method previewed Thursday.

segments.commentary: The starting gun: a one-line post and an image that interpretability people treated as pure delight.
Two days later the library arrived, with Haiku rating neurons by weirdness and combinations producing results like a humble muffin.
Not everything was cute: one poster shared a recipe for steering a single neuron to get an 'evil' Qwen.
Thursday brought a method for reading neurons directly rather than steering them, and Friday a one-neuron owl alongside the week's key caveat about what steering actually shows.
The week closed with the full database and tools, covering most layers of Qwen 3 8B and Gemma 4 12B.

tweets.name: a9lim
tweets.text:
@treetowntree and i created neuron lens: a database of every single neuron and attention head in qwen 3 8b and gemma 4 12b read using the R-lens (a J-lens variant) and what we call the "S-lens". you can find it at https://t.co/DI2Cpajc3M, along with the tools we used to make it. 

using the R-lens to read neurons' input and output projections turns out to be very effective at determining what a neuron does. we're able to legibly read what a majority of neurons do when fired: the lens qualitatively predicts the result of steering over 90% of the time!

the same trick lets us read attention heads' QK circuits and OV circuits, showing us both what they attend to and what they do with it. however, the R-lens has two important flaws: its accuracy degrades in early layers, and it can't separate the MLP block and the attention block.

we found ways around both these issues. we first modified the r-lens by fitting it on input tokens rather than output tokens to get the s-lens, which is accurate in early layers but inaccurate in late layers. we then fitted R- and S-lenses to the activations after attention but before the MLP to get "mid-lenses", which are much better at deciphering MLP inputs and attention outputs. using both of these techniques, we were able to interpret most of the models' layers.

stories.title: Patrick Stewart has sadly passed away at the age of 86
stories.overview: The death of Star Trek's Captain Picard and X-Men's Charles Xavier was announced from his own account on Thursday, by far the most-liked event of the week. stories.title: Agent swarms patch a compromised certificate, GMO's servers are hacked, and Binance reportedly loses $5.6B
stories.overview: The breach wave kept rolling. On Monday @theproteindance described 70 agents patching software hit by the compromised eMuhdra certificate while a GMO Internet hack drained FX accounts at over 70 brokerages, and a viral grid-attack 'whistleblower' was widely called fake. Friday brought a reported $5.6 billion Binance hack, a Polymarket shutdown after a third-party compromise, and an Epoch AI study showing an open model building Firefox exploits for about $1,000 each.
stories.connection: Both days cover the same continuing run of AI-era security incidents, and the Epoch study offered evidence for Monday's fear that cheap AI cognition is fuelling attacks.
stories.continuityNote: Last week's PHP-bug breaches gave way to a compromised certificate authority, exchange-scale crypto theft and hard evidence of open models writing working browser exploits.

tweets.name: Epoch AI
tweets.text:
In recent experiments, we found that GLM 5.3 can autonomously compromise recent versions of Mozilla Firefox using security fixes that have been published but not yet shipped to users.

We used a deliberately basic setup meant to emulate a relatively unsophisticated attacker with limited resources. After basic initial instructions to inspect those not-yet-shipped fixes, the model reliably built successful exploits for six recent Firefox versions on its own using only information available at the time of release.

These exploits, which cost about $1,000 per compromised version, would let an attacker steal passwords and authentication cookies stored in the browser, or read any files on the user's computer, after the user opens a single webpage, with no further interaction.

The exploits make use of the "patch gap," the time between when security fixes are made public in beta or "nightly" software updates and when those fixes are generally released to users. Until now, exploiting it required significant human time and skill, or special access to frontier models with advanced cyber capabilities.

Our results show that widely available open-weight models can now do this relatively cheaply and quickly. We gave GLM 5.3 up to 48 hours to find an exploit, but its fastest attempt needed only 12 hours.

In all of its successful attacks, the patch gap gave GLM 5.3 an initial foothold in the browser. To turn that foothold into reading files off the user's computer, the model also independently discovered and used a previously unpublished vulnerability.

We shared our findings with Mozilla, which patched the vulnerability in its October 27 Firefox 159.0 release. We haven't yet confirmed whether the attack still succeeds without it, but expect the fix makes it substantially harder. We're grateful to Mozilla for their responsiveness and collaboration.

stories.title: Anthropic files its S-1, warns no insurer could cover its risk, and the timeline counts future staff fortunes

tweets.name: Colossus
tweets.text:
The people of Silicon Valley are unwell.

If you work at a frontier lab or decacorn, you’ve got it bad. You haven’t seen your kids, your girlfriend’s annoyed, invites from friends to hang out are waning, even weddings are on hold. This is the time to make your mark and make your money, after all.

If you’re building a startup that’s trying to compete with or be one of these companies, you’ve got it bad. Maybe you passed up a job offer at one a couple years back, which means you left $100M on the table, you fucking idiot. Being an underdog isn't as fun as you thought.

If you’re working on a pre-AI startup, you’ve got it bad. Not too long ago you were the belle of the ball, but now your 30% year-on-year growth doesn’t feel like growth at all. It feels like death.

"Too many of my friends are spiraling," Brie Wolfson writes. "I don’t know how we’re supposed to live and work like this."

It’s all too much, too fast. Too much money, too much growth, too much power, too much change. Every month, a new frontier model is released. Every day, a new unicorn is minted. Seriously. 300 days into the year 2026, and 311 unicorns have been minted so far.

So what’s left for the sane ones? Brie went looking for teams playing a different game. She found one in Ottawa: a search infrastructure company that many of the AI darlings rely on.

It's growing fast, and its people are well.

Read @zebriez’s latest company dispatch from inside the sane asylum of turbopuffer.
